ranges.en: Opening claim: thirty-six Torah cases of intercourse-type prohibitions where intentional violation incurs karet.
Lists the first prohibitions: mother, father's wife, daughter-in-law, a male partner, and an animal.
A woman who brings an animal upon herself is liable to karet.
Liability for relations with a woman and her daughter, or with a married woman.
Liability for relations with one's sister.
Liability for relations with one's father's sister.
Liability for relations with one's mother's sister.
Liability for relations with one's wife's sister.
Liability for relations with one's brother's wife.
Liability for relations with the wife of one's father's brother.
Liability for relations with the wife of one's mother's brother.
Liability for relations with a menstruating woman.
Second list begins: blasphemer, idol worshipper, and one who gives offspring to Molekh.
Continues the list: giving seed to Molekh and the necromancer.
Liability for desecrating Shabbat.
Liability for an impure person who eats sacred food or enters the Temple while impure.
Liability for eating forbidden fat, consuming blood, eating notar or piggul.
Liability for slaughtering offerings and offering them outside the Temple.
Liability for eating leavened bread on Passover.
Liability for eating or performing forbidden labor on Yom Kippur.
Liability for blending anointing oil or incense in the prohibited manner.
Liability for applying the anointing oil to one's skin.
Names the two positive mitzvot, Passover offering and circumcision, whose failure incurs karet.
Positive commandments are listed; liability to karet applies for their intentional neglect.
For unwitting violation, one must bring a sin offering.
For doubtful violation, one brings a provisional guilt offering.
Exception for defiling the Temple, which requires a sliding-scale offering; attributed to Rabbi Meir.
The Rabbis dissent: the blasphemer is also liable to karet.
The Rabbis cite Numbers 15:29 to exclude the blasphemer, who sins by speech rather than by action.

ranges.en: Asks why the mishna needs to state a numbered tally of karet cases.
Rabbi Yohanan: the tally shows that one who commits all of them in one lapse of awareness is liable for each.
Raises a mishna on primary categories of labor and asks why its tally is stated.
Quoted mishna: the primary categories of labor number thirty-nine, forty less one.
Asks again why the tally of labor categories is stated.
Same reasoning: all labors done in one lapse of awareness each create a separate liability.
Raises a mishna on four people who require atonement and asks why the tally is stated.
Quoted mishna: those who have not yet completed atonement may not eat sacrificial meat.
Asks why the mishna gives a tally of four such people.
The tally excludes Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view that a convert makes a fifth such person.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says a convert needs a sprinkled offering before eating sacrificial meat.
Hence the mishna says four, excluding the fifth person.
Raises a mishna on four who bring offerings for intentional violations and asks why the tally is stated.
Quoted mishna: for intentional violations they bring offerings as for unwitting ones.
Asks why this tally of four is needed.
The tally excludes Rabbi Shimon's view.
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon holds that an intentional false oath about a deposit receives no atonement.
Hence the mishna lists four, including the deposit oath.
Raises a mishna on five people who bring one offering for several transgressions and asks why the tally is stated.
Quoted mishna: these five bring one offering for multiple transgressions of the same kind.
Asks why the tally of five is needed.
The mishna lists the tally in order to teach its final clause about the nazirite.
Explains the nazirite case: he becomes impure again on the seventh day after purification.
Asks whose opinion this is, namely Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda.
Yes: his view holds that the naziriteship of purity takes effect from the seventh day.
Objects that on Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view the nazirite case cannot arise, since the vow starts on day eight.
Explains that a seventh-day recurrence counts as one continuous impurity under that view.
An eighth-day recurrence yields separate offerings, so the mishna must follow Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda.
Asks for the scriptural source of each of the two opinions.
Baraita on Numbers 6:11: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi reads the verse as the eighth day, Rabbi Yosei as the shaving day.
Raises another mishna with a tally of five and asks why it is stated.
Quoted mishna: five people bring a sliding-scale offering.
Asks why the tally of five sliding-scale offerings is stated.
Excludes Rabbi Eliezer's view that a king brings a goat for defiling the Temple.
Raises a mishna on four primary categories of damage and asks why the tally is stated.
Excludes Rabbi Oshaya's view that there are thirteen categories of damage.
Asks why Rabbi Oshaya's tally is needed.
Excludes Rabbi Hiyya's view that there are twenty-four categories of damage.
Asks why Rabbi Hiyya's tally is needed.
Excludes an informer and a priest who renders an offering piggul from the damage categories.
Restates the Master's earlier point: one lapse of awareness yields liability for each prohibition.
Objects that one cannot say a person who violates all of them is entirely exempt.
Cites Leviticus 18:29, that all these abominations incur karet, to support liability.
Proposes instead that one is liable only once when he violates everything in one lapse.
Rabbi Yohanan: karet for intercourse with a sister is singled out to separate the prohibitions.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye objects: the sister case alone should yield a separate liability.
Objects: does Rav Beivai not accept the principle of a singled-out item within a generalization?
Baraita: a singled-out item within a generalization teaches its halakha for the whole category.
Baraita cites Leviticus 7:20 on impure consumption of peace offerings.
Asks why peace offerings were singled out if they were already part of the sacred category.
Singling them out links all altar offerings to them, excluding Temple maintenance items.
Rav Beivai replies that the baraita's exclusion of Temple maintenance items applies only to its own case.
Explains: a sister is forbidden for life, unlike a married woman who may be divorced.
R. Yona's reply upholds Rabbi Yohanan's view against Rav Beivai's married-woman exclusion.
Cites Leviticus 18:29 as a juxtaposition linking all forbidden relations to the sister case.
Explains the juxtaposition: each forbidden relation incurs its own liability, as the sister does.
Objects from Rabbi Yitzhak's view that all karet cases are included, so the sister verse needs another purpose.
Asks where Rabbi Yitzhak derives separate liability for each prohibition.
Derives it from Leviticus 18:19, whose lengthy phrasing separates each woman.
Asks why the Rabbis, too, could not derive it from the same verse.
Yes, the Rabbis could derive it from that verse as well.
Asks what purpose the specific sister karet verse then serves.
The Rabbis need it to separate sister, father's sister, and mother's sister.
Asks why separation is needed, since these are distinct persons and categories.
The verse separates one act that violates three prohibitions, requiring three offerings.
Asks where Rabbi Yitzhak derives this point.
From the latter clause of Leviticus 20:17, which states that his sister's nakedness is uncovered.
Asks what the Rabbis do with the repeated 'his sister' in the latter clause.
They require it to teach the separate liabilities.

ranges.en: Explains the verse's purpose: the sister who is both paternal and maternal shows punishment is not derived by a fortiori reasoning.
Rabbi Yitzhak holds that punishment may be derived by a fortiori reasoning.
Alternatively, Rabbi Yitzhak derives the karet from the warning of the prohibition itself.
Rabbi Elazar in Rabbi Hoshaya's name: where two prohibitions share one karet, divide the sin offering between them.
Asks what example illustrates this principle.
The example: blending the anointing oil and applying it to the skin.
Cites Exodus 30:32 forbidding application of the oil to human flesh and its compounding.
Notes that a single karet covers both prohibitions.
Cites Exodus 30:33 on compounding the oil and placing it upon a stranger, carrying one karet.
Objects: if prohibitions are separate and Leviticus 18:29 applies karet to all, why is the sister karet written separately?
The Rabbis need the verse for the rule against a fortiori punishment; Rabbi Yitzhak uses it to make one liable for the sister who is both paternal and maternal.
Asks where the Rabbis derive this halakha from.
Rabbi Yitzhak holds that 'his sister' in the first clause is verse style, so the latter clause separates the prohibitions.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzhak: our mishna teaches the same kind of blending and applying cases.
Quoted mishna: blending the anointing oil, blending the incense, and applying the anointing oil to the skin.
Asks why this baraita is needed.
Baraita: the incense clause placed in the middle teaches that incense is an independent prohibition.
Explains: incense blending is independent, so the oil blending and oil application are also separately liable.
Objects: if the tanna wished to group the blends together, he could have reversed the order of the clauses.
The hypothetical reordered version of the mishna.
Asks why the mishna splits the oil clauses with the incense clause in between.
This teaches a separation between the prohibitions, so two sin offerings are required.
Quoted mishna: one who has intercourse with a male.
Asks by what criteria the tanna tallies the prohibitions.
Elaborates the difficulty: a tally of men or of women would leave out one or two cases of karet.
Rabbi Yohanan: the tanna counts men only, and teaches the case in a revised form.
Rabbi Yohanan's revised clause: a male who lies with a male and brings a male upon him, liable for two per Rabbi Yishmael.
Objects: since the latter clause follows Rabbi Akiva on blasphemy, the first clause may also follow him.
Suggests the mishna follows Rabbi Akiva throughout, except that the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael.
Refutes: Rabbi Abbahu stated that per Rabbi Yishmael the case is liable twice.
Rabbi Yishmael derives two prohibitions from two verses, Leviticus 18:22 and Deuteronomy 23:18.
Rabbi Akiva holds that only one sin offering applies.
Rabbi Akiva derives both prohibitions from one verse, read as both active and passive.
Resolution: the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael, and the blasphemy case follows Rabbi Akiva.
Objects: if so, the tanna should also list the bestiality cases.
Abaye: even per Rabbi Yishmael, bestiality yields one sin offering, since 'sodomite' is written only for men.
Rabbi Elazar in Rav's name: thirty-three sin offerings plus three extra karetot complete the list.
Asks why the latter clause mentions Passover and circumcision.
Objects: perhaps they are listed to require an offering, but an offering is not brought for omitting them.
Baraita: the whole Torah is juxtaposed to idolatry, in Numbers 15:29-30, as an unwitting sin of action.
Like idolatry, only sit-and-refrain prohibitions require a sin offering for unwitting violation, not omissions.
Restates: thirty-three sin offerings for unwitting acts, with three karetot completing the list.
Mishna: one who desecrates Shabbat; the Sages say the primary labors number forty-less-one.
Rabbi Yohanan: the tanna means unwitting Shabbat with intentional labors, which yields only one offering.
Baraita confirms one offering for unwitting Shabbat with intentional labors.
Objects: the tanna should have taught intentional Shabbat with unwitting labors, yielding forty-less-one offerings.
Baraita on Leviticus 4:2 (me'aḥat mehena): sometimes one offering covers all, sometimes one per violation.
Baraita: the 'hena' case is intentional Shabbat with unwitting labors.
The tanna prefers the unwitting-Shabbat case because it still requires a sin offering.
Likewise with idolatry: unwitting worship with intentional rites still requires one offering.
Asks what unwitting idol worship looks like; bowing in a house thought to be a synagogue involves no transgression.
Asks about bowing to a king's statue: intention decides between stoning and no offense.
Proposes bowing out of love or fear of the one demanding it, as an unwitting transgression.
Abaye's view works here, but for Rava, who exempts that case, what is the unwitting example?

ranges.en: Rather, the case is one who thinks idol worship is permitted, so the unwitting act stems from ignorance.
Notes that Rava raised his dilemma before Rav Nachman only regarding Shabbat.
Rava's dilemma: is one unaware of both Shabbat and its labors liable to one or two sin offerings?
Complete exemption was not the subject of Rava's question.
Rav Pappa: unwitting idolatry arises with a captive child who knows idolatry is forbidden but not these particular objects.
Alternatively, the case may be an adult who misread the verse about gods of silver and gold.
Cites Exodus 20:20 on gods of silver and gold.
He thinks bowing is forbidden only to silver or gold idols, so it is unwitting idolatry with intentional rites.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika, in Rav Beivai's name: the tanna teaches general categories of Shabbat and idolatry.
Asks what the inference is from the mishna's wording.
Quoted mishna: one who has intercourse with a woman and her daughter, or with a married woman.
Objects: the daughter of a raped woman is not listed, though it falls within the category.
The Sages reply: the mishna teaches only prohibitions written explicitly, not those derived from verses.
Objects: the wife's daughter and grandchildren are written explicitly yet unlisted, so general categories must be meant.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika notes a contradiction within Rav Beivai bar Abaye's statements.
Cites the ruling that one who offers limbs of a Temple-slaughtered offering outside the Temple is liable.
Rav Beivai's difficulty: the mishna's thirty-six cases become thirty-seven if these are counted.
Rav Aha asks: why not answer that the tanna teaches the category of offering up?
The cases differ: Shabbat and idolatry are detailed in their own tractates, while offering up is not.
Rav Yirmeya asks Rav Zeira about two karetot for one prohibition.
Zeira: slaughtering and offering up are two separate prohibitions, so the case does not match.
By verbal analogy both acts are written explicitly, and punishment requires an explicit prohibition.
Cites Deuteronomy 12:14 on sacrificing burnt offerings in the designated place.
Juxtaposition links slaughtering to offering up, so neither is punished without an explicit prohibition.
Zeira asks: perhaps the case is two death-penalty prohibitions with one prohibition written for both?
Zeira: the case is the necromancer and the sorcerer, both of whom face death penalties.
Baraita from Sanhedrin: a necromancer and a sorcerer are listed for stoning.
Objects: why does the stoning list include the sorcerer while the karet list does not?
Rabbi Yohanan: both are stated in one prohibition, so they are not counted separately.
Asks why the tanna did not state the sorcerer instead of the necromancer.
The verse opens with the necromancer, so that case is the one listed.
Reish Lakish: the sorcerer's case involves no action, only speech through a bone.
Asks why Reish Lakish does not follow Rabbi Yohanan's explanation.
Rav Pappa: the verse separates the two death penalties, but separate death penalties do not create separate offerings.
Asks why Rabbi Yohanan does not follow Reish Lakish's explanation.
The karet tanna is Rabbi Akiva, who holds that action is not required.
Reish Lakish: Rabbi Akiva requires a minor action, though not a major one.
Asks what action a necromancer performs.
Striking the arms together to raise the dead counts as an action.
Asks what action the blasphemer performs.
Twisting the lips while speaking counts as an action.
Hypothesis: striking the arms is a minor action even according to the Rabbis.
Baraita: idolatry requires an action such as sacrifice or bowing, yet bowing involves no action.
Reish Lakish: the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who requires no action.
Rabbi Yohanan: even according to the Rabbis, bending one's height is an action.
Infers that Reish Lakish holds bending is no action per the Rabbis, so striking the arms should not count either.
Reish Lakish speaks only per Rabbi Akiva; per the Rabbis, striking the arms is not an action.
Asks why the mishna excludes the blasphemer for lacking action, if the necromancer also lacks one.
Suggests listing both the blasphemer and the necromancer as exclusions.
The tanna teaches one of two possible exclusions.
Asks why the tanna should not list the necromancer and omit the blasphemer.
The blasphemer is listed to rule out that the Rabbis concede to Akiva, since his karet appears beside an offering.
Ulla: the necromancer's action is burning incense to a demon.
Rava objects: then the necromancer is an idolater, already listed in the mishna.
Rava: he burns incense to a demon to gather demons together, by sorcery.
Abaye objects: then he is a gatherer, which is a prohibition without karet.
Rava: the Torah counts this gatherer among necromancers, punishable by stoning and also by karet.
Abaye asks what the gatherer prohibition is, if it carries no karet.
Rava cites a baraita: one who gathers large beasts, small beasts, snakes and scorpions is liable.
Abaye rules: gathering a hornet and scorpion by sorcery is forbidden, unless they are chasing him.
Raises an objection based on Rabbi Yohanan's view that bending one's height counts as an action.

ranges.en: Twisting the lips counts as an action, though Rava exempts blasphemy, which lies primarily in the heart.
Rabbi Zeira objects: conspiring witnesses, who sin by speech, are not obligated for an unwitting offering since no action is involved.
Asks why the witnesses' speech, which the verse ties to the mouth, does not count as an action.
Rava: conspiring witnesses differ because their sin lies primarily in what they saw, which is not an action.
Mishna: one who eats forbidden fat is liable to karet.
Baraita on Leviticus 7:23: each type of forbidden fat, from ox, sheep, or goat, carries its own liability.
Rabbi Yishmael holds three sets of lashes; the Sages hold only one.
Suggests the dispute: Yishmael flogs for a general prohibition, while the Rabbis do not.
The Rabbis: one is not flogged for violating a general prohibition.
Yishmael also rejects flogging for general prohibitions; here the superfluous words teach separate liability.
The Rabbis: naming ox, sheep, and goat excludes the fats of undomesticated animals, which would otherwise be forbidden.
Suggests Yishmael's reasoning: without the other animals named, each would be needed, so each separates a liability.
The Rabbis: had the verse named only an ox, one might derive undomesticated animals from the Sinai command using behema.
Explains the hypothetical analogy to the Sinai command and why the verse names the three animals.
Suggests Yishmael's reasoning: had the verse said only sheep, all three words are needed to separate liabilities.
Alternative: had the verse said only goat, the other words are needed to separate liabilities.
The Rabbis: had the verse said only sheep, one would think only sheep fat is forbidden.
Asks what distinguishes sheep, such that one would think the prohibition applies only to them.
Baraita of Rabbi Hanina: Numbers 18:17 lists the burning of portions for firstborn ox, sheep, and goat separately.
Rabbi Hanina: with only an ox named, derivation to sheep and goat could be refuted, since the ox has more libations.
Likewise, with only a sheep named, derivation could be refuted by the sheep's distinctive tail.
Likewise, with only a goat named, the refutation is its role in idolatry offerings, so none can be derived from the others.
Deriving the ox from sheep and goat is refuted: sheep and goat are used for the Paschal offering.
Refutes a sheep derivation from ox and goat on the Paschal-offering point, so sheep must be written.
Refutes the goat derivation from ox and sheep: ox and goat feature in idolatry atonement offerings.
Ox and sheep each have an extra feature for the altar, so none can be derived from the other; all three are needed.
Objects: why not write all fat and stay silent, if naming the three animals only permits undomesticated fat?
The verse on forbidden fat appears in the context of sacrificial animals, and that context shapes the derivation.
Objects: the Rabbis would then reject derivation from context, which is an accepted principle of exegesis.
All accept derivation from context; the dispute is whether one prohibition's rules derive from another's, which Yishmael allows.
Cites Leviticus 3:17 on the perpetual statute against fat and blood, applied to sacrificial animals.
Sacrificial animals include no undomesticated animals, so the naming of ox, sheep, and goat separates each liability.
Hence ox, sheep, and goat are separate liabilities, each triggering liability for each one eaten.
Both prohibitions are derived from the karet verse in Leviticus 7:25, which separates each animal's fat.
The Rabbis: lashes-based prohibitions derive from lashes-based ones, but not from karet-based ones.
Alternatively, the Rabbis' reasoning is as Rav Mari said to Rav Zevid.
Rav Mari objects: then the tail of a non-sacred animal should be forbidden fat.
Rav Zevid replies, citing Leviticus 7:23 on the three animals.
The verse requires a fat common to all three animals; the tail is absent in ox and goat, so it is not forbidden.
So naming ox, sheep, and goat permits the tail of non-sacred animals and does not separate liabilities.
Rabbi Yishmael rejoins: then let the verse name only ox and sheep, so the goat must be separating a liability.
Rabbi Hanina: Yishmael concedes that for an offering only one sin offering is brought.
Asks why, since this case does not match the prohibition of forbidden relations.
Baraita: eating the same fat in two lapses, or two types of fat in one lapse, each yields two sin offerings.
Rami bar Hama objects: why two offerings for two types in one lapse, since lapses should be separate?
Rav Hisda: the case is leftover fat, liable both for notar and for forbidden fat.
Rami objects: then he should also be liable for misusing sacred food.
Rav Sheshet: the case is forbidden fat of sacrificial animals, following Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Baraita: one who eats fat of a carcass or of sacrificial animals is liable to two sets of lashes.
Rabbi Yehuda: three lashes for fat of sacrificial animals; Western sages laughed at this, and the Gemara reinterprets it per Yishmael.

ranges.en: Asks why the baraita cannot be read per Rabbi Yishmael.
Rabbi Hanina: Yishmael concedes that only one sin offering is brought for these violations.
Cites Rabbi Eliezer: Rabbi Yehuda concedes that for sacrificial fat only one sin offering is brought.
Reish Lakish: the case is fat eaten from two dishes, following Rabbi Yehoshua, so each dish is a separate act.
Baraita: carcass fat yields two lashes; sacrificial fat yields two, or three per Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Sheizevi asks Rava about the reasoning behind the number of lashes.
On Rabbi Yehuda's view, three verses yield three prohibitions: two on sacrificial fat and one on non-priests.
Asks the reasoning of the Rabbis, who would yield only two lashes.
The Rabbis: the perpetual-statute verse concerns sacrificial animals, while the ox verse concerns non-sacred animals.
Had the verse mentioned only sacrifices, one would exclude non-sacred fat, so the ox verse is needed.
Had the verse mentioned only ox, one would exclude sacrificial fat, since its meat was permitted; both verses are needed.
Rabbi Yehuda: the ox verse is written in the context of sacrificial animals.
Objects: then the Rabbis would reject derivation from context, a basic exegetical principle.
Everyone accepts context-based derivation; the dispute is whether a karet-based prohibition can be derived from others.
Asks why Rabbi Yehuda needs the fat-and-blood verse if he already derived the fat prohibition.
Baraita: Leviticus 3:17 juxtaposes blood to fat; Rabbi Yehuda gives blood two lashes, the Sages one warning.
Asks why juxtaposition is needed, since fat already has two verses.
Cites Leviticus 7:26 as a second prohibition on blood, covering fowl and animal.
Rather, the baraita teaches that blood's juxtaposition yields three lashes, like fat.
Asks why fat is known to carry three lashes without juxtaposition.
Blood's juxtaposition is needed so that blood is not excluded from the non-priest prohibition by analogy to impurity.
Asks why the juxtaposition matters for the Rabbis, who hold only one prohibition on blood.
Explains that it serves the baraita that follows on combining fat and blood with flesh.
Baraita: fat is discrete from its flesh and does not combine with it; blood is likewise, except creeping animals' blood.
Asks whether this is derived from the fat-and-blood verse or from another verse.
Cites Leviticus 11:29 on the blood and flesh of creeping animals combining.
Without juxtaposition one might limit combination to impurity; the juxtaposition teaches it applies to consumption too.
Ravina: therefore a snake's blood and flesh combine to make an olive-bulk.
Asks what Ravina is teaching, since this is the same derivation from juxtaposition.
A snake is not included in impurity, so the juxtaposition teaches that all non-discrete blood combines in consumption.
Rava asks what the three karet mentions for blood concern.
One for non-sacred blood, one for sacred blood, and one for exudate blood.
Baraita: exudate blood carries a prohibition, and Rabbi Yehuda holds karet applies to it.
Asks what the third karet is for, per the Rabbis, who deny karet for exudate.
Even per Rabbi Yehuda, karet for exudate is derived from the superfluous phrase any manner of blood.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda derives karet for non-sacred and exudate blood from any manner of blood in Leviticus 17:10.
Rather, Rava's karet verses cover non-sacred, sacred, and covering blood.
Asks why there are five prohibitions stated with regard to blood.
Each prohibition covers a distinct blood type: non-sacred, sacred, covering, limb blood, and exudate.
Rabbi Illa: one who eats the tithes of grain, wine, and oil outside Jerusalem is flogged three times.
Objects: one is not flogged for a general prohibition, and this one covers all of these categories.
Here the verses are superfluous, so the case is different.
Asks why the verse permitting tithes inside the chosen place needs a separate verse prohibiting them outside.
That verse separates each tithe type, so one is liable to lashes for each.
Objects: if derived from the positive command, one might limit the lashes to positive commands, not prohibitions.

ranges.en: Gemara frames the verse as a prohibition on eating second tithe outside Jerusalem
Objection that this is a general prohibition covering all kinds, so listing them seems superfluous
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that eating bread, parched grain or fresh stalks before the omer incurs three lashes
Objection: one is not flogged for violating a general prohibition
Reply: this case differs because the verses are superfluous and must be specified
Proposal to derive the other grains from bread, which the Gemara then questions
Explains the refutation: bread is unique in its increased halla obligation
Proposal to derive bread and stalks from parched grain alone
Refutation: parched grain is unadulterated while bread has been processed
Refutation: fresh stalks cannot be derived since parched grain has increased meal-offering obligation
Proposal to derive bread and parched grain from fresh stalks, with a refutation to follow
Refutation: fresh stalks are unique in being wholly unchanged from their original state
Conclusion: two of the three cannot be derived from one, but one can be derived from two
Proposal to omit bread and derive it from parched grain and stalks
Refutation: parched grain and stalks are unadulterated relative to bread
Proposal to omit stalks and derive them from bread and parched grain
Refutation: bread and parched grain have increased meal-offering obligation
Rabbi Yitzchak could reply that the verse need not write parched grain
Asks what the refutation of this alternative would be
Gives refutations: halla status and unchanged state each show the other factor is not decisive
Concludes one is flogged for each type because the verse is superfluous
Objection: parched grain alone should carry separate liability, the others a single set
Proposal to write the three kinds in different orders to show each liability
Asks why parched grain is written in the middle of the list
Explains the middle placement teaches that bread and stalks each incur parched grain's punishment
Rabbi Yannai teaches that a verbal analogy is a fundamental principle; piggul karet is derived only by analogy
Rabbi Yohanan cites Zavda bar Levi's teaching linking notar in Leviticus 19:8
Quotes Leviticus 7:18 linking the same liability wording to piggul
Concludes that just as notar incurs karet, so does piggul, from the matching wording
Rabbi Simai repeats that verbal analogy is fundamental, teaching the karet for notar through analogy
Asks what the verbal analogy is
Links sacred in Leviticus 19:8 with sacred in Exodus 29:34 to show the verse concerns notar
Abaye teaches that the analogy on intercourse with a raped woman's daughter is fundamental
Rava cites the analogy of henna and lewdness to derive death by burning
Rav Ashi teaches that the list of stoning cases is a fundamental principle taught by analogy
Baraita links their blood in the necromancer case with stoning, supporting the analogy
Quotes the mishnah on one who compounds the anointing oil
Baraita: compounding oil to teach it, or to give it to the public, is exempt; liability is only for Moses' oil
Restates the rule that compounding to teach, or to hand to the public, is exempt
Asks from where this rule is derived
Derives the rule by analogy between the anointing oil and the incense formula
Reads the verse as prohibiting only making it for oneself, so giving to the public is exempt
Applies the same public-giving exemption to oil and incense
Derives incense from oil by analogy: compounding in halves is exempt
Challenge: Rava says incense compounded in halves is liable
Oil compounded in halves is exempt
Rava's reply: the verse forbids only the whole formula, so halves are permitted for oil, not incense
Verse on incense making implies it is compounded twice daily, morning and evening
Baraita lists the ingredients of the anointing oil and their total weight
Gemara asks why the baraita does not say kaneh bosem like kinnamon bosem
Argues that the stated quantities would then total two thousand, which conflicts with the count
Suggests the verse should state the halves explicitly

Shows from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's views and the baraita on peace offering fat that a prohibition takes effect on sacrificial food.
Objects that a baraita from Rabbi Shimon says piggul and notar do not apply to items ascending the altar.
Suggests Rabbi Shimon's view is a tannaitic dispute, with some holding he accepts stacked prohibitions on sacrificial food.
Challenges the view that denies stacked prohibitions, asking how it handles the verse that all fat is the Lord's.
Interprets the verse as referring to offspring of sacrificial animals, sanctified at birth, when both prohibitions take effect together.
Mishna opening: a provisional offering whose ram is found unneeded before slaughter goes free, per Rabbi Meir.
Mishna: the Rabbis treat the disqualified provisional ram as a blemished offering sold for Temple gifts, while Rabbi Eliezer sacrifices it.
Mishna on discovery after slaughter, blood collection or sprinkling, and Rabbi Yosei's view on blood still in the cup.
Mishna contrasts the definite guilt offering, which goes free before slaughter and is buried or burned after slaughter.
Mishna on an ox sentenced to stoning and on a heifer whose neck is broken, with the same before-or-after distinctions.
Mishna on the heifer of a found corpse, whose neck is broken once its uncertainty atones, so its mitzva is fulfilled.
Asks what Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree about in the provisional ram case.
Rabbi Meir holds the sanctity lapses once the need is gone, while the Rabbis hold initial sanctification stands.
Baraita: the dispute concerns a case where it became known he sinned or did not sin.
Explains Rabbi Meir's far-reaching view in the sinned case: the animal goes free because at designation he did not know.
Explains the Rabbis' far-reaching view in the not-sinned case: his heart struck him, so the sanctity remains.
Rav Sheshet says Rabbi Meir concedes to the Rabbis.

ranges.en: Restates the case of one who designates two provisional offerings as backup and atones with one; the other is sold for gift offerings.
Asks what the reason is that Rabbi Meir agrees in the case of two designated animals.
Rabbi Meir's dispute applies only to self-designated offerings, and the backup designation reveals the same pangs of conscience.
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that the Rabbis concede to Rabbi Meir where the witnesses were later proven conspiring.
The Rabbis dispute Rabbi Meir only for self-designated offerings; where witnesses prompted the designation, he expected other witnesses to refute them.
Rava objects from the stoned ox mishna, where the Rabbis agree the animal goes free when the testimony is found false.
Rava suggests the mishna refers to conspiring witnesses, which would then undercut the Rabbis' ruling on the guilt offering.
Abaye replies that the ox case concerns a supposed victim appearing alive, so Rava's proof does not hold.
The guilt offering case is not parallel: an offering designated because of witnesses lacks wholehearted resolve, so it goes free.
Rav Yehuda and Rava disagree on the Rabbi Elazar view that a witness-prompted offering is like a sota's meal offering and goes free.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that the witness-prompted offering must graze until blemished and then sold for gift offerings.
Objects that by Rabbi Yohanan one should compare the case to the sota's meal offering, as Rabbi Elazar did.
The sota offering clarifies sin and is not for atonement, but a guilt offering atones, so the wholehearted resolve keeps it sacred.
Rabbi Keruspedai says Rabbi Yohanan holds that anyone who takes an ox sentenced to stoning acquires it after the witnesses were exposed.
Rava explains: the owner relinquishes only if told a witness accused his ox; if he is accused himself, he will seek counter-witnesses.
Asks how this differs from Reish Lakish's ruling on an idolatrous city, whose property anyone may take once witnesses are exposed.
In an idolatrous city each resident relinquishes ownership because others sinned; in the ox case the owner knows his own innocence and keeps title.
Reish Lakish: when a gift recipient says he does not want the gift, anyone who takes it acquires it, since ownership was relinquished.
Asks how this differs from the teaching attributed to Rav Sheshet on gifts a recipient declares void after receiving them.
Rav Sheshet holds that a recipient who says he does not want the gift makes it void, while saying it is void alone accomplishes nothing.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether his statement is effective means the gift returns to the giver, which would contradict Reish Lakish.
His statement is effective means the giver also does not acquire it, so anyone who takes it acquires it.
A baraita says a partner who says my hand is removed from the field has said nothing, contradicting Reish Lakish.
That baraita differs: removal refers only to legal dealings, not to the field itself.
A baraita on a dying man's gift of slaves, refused by the recipient, has the first owner's heirs acquire them per Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds a gift is given only with intent to be accepted, so refusal returns it to the giver.
Objects that the first tanna's ruling would make the refused slaves non-priests eating teruma, contradicting Reish Lakish.
The first tanna holds a renounced slave is emancipated but needs a bill of manumission, so he may eat teruma while still held.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer says a provisional offering discovered unneeded before slaughter is sacrificed for another sin.
Asks why Rabbi Eliezer needs another sin, since he elsewhere allows volunteering provisional offerings daily.
Rav Ashi says the mishna follows the view of those who advised Bava ben Buta to wait for a true uncertainty.
Mishna: a provisional offering whose flesh is discovered unneeded after slaughter is burned, implying slaughtered non-sacred animals in the courtyard are burned.
Raises a contradiction from the later mishna, where such a case is buried, so the two rulings conflict.
Rabbi Elazar says the mishna is disjointed; Rabba says the definite and provisional cases differ in consecration.
Presses that the definite guilt offering contradiction stands, so the mishna must be disjointed with differing authors.
Rav Ashi says burning applies because a provisional offering looks like a disqualified offering, and a definite one after sprinkling also.
Mishna: if blood was sprinkled before discovery of no sin and the meat is intact, the priests may eat it.
Asks why the meat may be eaten, since the offerer now knows he did not sin.
Rava cites the verse he did not know and he is forgiven, so he lacked knowledge at the moment of atonement.
Mishna: Rabbi Yosei says that even blood still in the cup is sprinkled and the meat eaten.
Asks why Rabbi Yosei has the blood sprinkled, since knowledge exists at the moment of forgiveness.
Rava says Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Shimon, that blood ready to be sprinkled is treated as already sprinkled.
Objects that Rabbi Shimon's principle applies only to certain sprinkling, and cites a Western view on the service vessel.
Mishna on the heifer with broken neck, and the amoraim's dispute on when benefit from it is prohibited, Rav Hamnuna or Rava.
Asks when, on Rav Hamnuna's view, the prohibition takes effect, since Rava's view is clear.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yannai reports a forgotten answer on the stage when the heifer becomes prohibited; the Sages suggest its descent to the stream.
Rav Hamnuna says the prohibition starts while the heifer is alive, citing the Hullin mishna on slaughtering a heifer whose neck is broken.
Rav Hamnuna explains: Rabbi Shimon holds slaughter that does not make the animal fit is not slaughter, so he is exempt.
If the prohibition only started after the neck break, Rabbi Shimon's exemption would make no sense, since the slaughter would then make it fit.
Objects that Rabbi Shimon could hold breaking the neck by slaughter is valid, since a mishna says the two heifers are not interchangeable.
Rava was silent, and later reflects that he could have said Rabbi Shimon disagrees with that mishna.
Objects that Rav Hamnuna would reply the mishna would have mentioned such a tanna if it existed.
Rava's proof from the mishna: a heifer whose neck is to be broken goes free if found innocent before the break, so the prohibition starts later.
Rejects Rava's proof by re-reading the mishna's clauses with the fitness threshold, and raises a further difficulty from the latter clause.
Rava continues: the latter clause's atonement reasoning shows the prohibition takes effect only when the neck is broken.
Resolves that the mishna's ruling is a tannaitic dispute, supporting Rav Hamnuna's baraita on offerings that enable and atone.
Baraita: the heifer whose neck is broken is compared to the bird offering, so it is prohibited while still alive.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer says one may volunteer a provisional offering daily, and Bava ben Buta's offering history is recounted.
Bava ben Buta's oath, and the Rabbis' view that a provisional offering is brought only for real uncertainty of karet or sin offering.
Mishna: provisional offerings are not brought after Yom Kippur, since the whole day atones for uncertain sins.
Mishna: a woman's uncertain bird sin offering is brought after Yom Kippur and is buried if she is found exempt.
Asks the reason that Rabbi Eliezer allows volunteering a provisional offering every day.
If the offering were obligatory, a sin offering would be unnecessary afterwards, so the provisional offering must be a gift offering.
The Rabbis reply that burnt and peace offerings may be vows or gifts, while provisional offerings are obligatory and protect bodies from suffering.
Rav Aha son of Rava suggests a provisional offering may be a gift like burnt and peace offerings, which are sometimes obligatory.
Rav Ashi replies that burnt and peace offerings are primarily gift offerings, while provisional offerings are primarily obligatory like sin offerings.
Rabbi Hiyya teaches a baraita before Rava, and the page ends with this new teaching.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava objects: the mishna limits provisional offerings to karet-liable sins, and Rabbi Eliezer's gift view does not fit the carcass case.
Rabbi Hiyya reports Rabba's reply: the baraita follows the Bava ben Buta sages, not Rabbi Eliezer's gift view.
Asks the reason for the Bava ben Buta sages' view that a provisional offering covers any uncertain sin.
The verse about any of the mitzvot that may not be done shows a provisional offering covers any sin.
Asks the reason for the Rabbis' limit of provisional offerings to karet-liable sins.
The Rabbis derive the limit by verbal analogy with the word mitzvot in the standard sin offering for forbidden fat.
Explains the analogy: the provisional offering applies only where the sin is karet if intentional and a sin offering if unwitting.
Baraita: five guilt offerings atone, while a provisional guilt offering does not atone completely.
Asks what the tanna of the baraita means by this.
Rav Yosef explains: the five guilt offerings atone fully, while a provisional offering needs a sin offering if the sin later becomes known.
The baraita does not follow Rabbi Eliezer; Ravina says the five offerings require the sin to be known, while provisional ones do not.
Mishna: those liable for sin offerings and definite guilt offerings after Yom Kippur must bring them, while provisional ones are exempt.
Asks from where it is derived that Yom Kippur does not atone for sins requiring offerings.
Verse on Yom Kippur atoning for transgressions and sins: sins subject to offerings are not atoned by the day.
Abaye objects that the verse refers only to the inner goat, which does not atone for known violations.
Abaye derives the limit from the scapegoat verse, where sins are juxtaposed with transgressions, so offering-atoned sins are excluded.
Rav Dimi objects that the mishna's four intentional sin-offering cases show such transgressions can be atoned by offerings.
Reish Lakish's view, transmitted by Ravin, derives the same limit from the scapegoat verse.
Rav Dimi's difficulty is repeated; Ravin argues most transgressions are not offering-atoned, and Abaye asks if majority is written.
Abaye infers from the verse on iniquities that refers to intentional sins, and from the juxtaposition that the scapegoat atones only for offering-free sins.
Mishna: those liable for provisional guilt offerings are exempt from bringing them after Yom Kippur.
Asks from where this rule is derived.
Rabbi Elazar derives it from the verse that Yom Kippur atones for sins known only to God, meaning uncertain sins.
Rav Tahlifa in Rava's name says the first clause cannot be proven by this, so the derivation is not convincing.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rejects explaining the halakha from either Rav Dimi's verse or Abaye's verse on transgressions.
Rabbi Elazar's verse: Yom Kippur atones for sins only God knows, not for sins the sinner is aware of.
Rav Tahlifa in Rava's name: those liable to lashes after Yom Kippur still receive them.
Asks what distinguishes lashes from sin offerings and guilt offerings, which must be brought after Yom Kippur.
Financial liabilities are not exempted by Yom Kippur, but the body-based lashes might be; Rav Tahlifa says that is not so.
Asks how Rava can say Yom Kippur does not exempt lashes, citing a Shevuot mishna.
Rava refers to a transgression with prior warning, while the mishna refers to one without warning.
Introduces the mnemonic listing the topics the Gemara will test: birth, leprosy, nazirite, sota and heifer.
Raises a difficulty: an uncertain woman who gave birth should not bring her offering after Yom Kippur, since God alone knows.
Rav Hoshaya says the verse atones for sins but not for impurity, and the birth offering is for purification.
Asks what can be said on Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's view that a woman who gave birth is a sinner.
Even for Rabbi Shimon the birth offering permits sacrificial food and does not atone, so it is brought after Yom Kippur.
Rav Ashi cites the mishna on the woman's bird offering, brought after Yom Kippur because it permits eating, not atones.
Objects that an uncertain leper's offering should lapse on the same logic, and cites the seven causes of leprosy, with Rabbi Oshaya's reply.
A leper's offering permits sacrificial food rather than atoning, so it is brought after Yom Kippur.
Objects that an uncertain nazirite's offering should likewise lapse, and repeats Rabbi Oshaya's verse answer.
Asks what can be said for Rabbi Elazar ben HaKappar's view that a nazirite is a sinner.
Even for him the nazirite's offering permits sacrificial food rather than atoning, so it is brought after Yom Kippur.
Objects that an uncertain sota's offering should lapse, and Rabbi Oshaya answers that her acts make her impure.
Abaye says the paramour knows of the sin; Rava says the sota's offering clarifies iniquity rather than atones.
Raises the heifer case: an uncertain murder unknown to God should not need the broken-neck heifer after Yom Kippur.
Abaye says the murderer knows; Rava cites the verse that blood requires blood; Rav Pappa cites the heifer prayer for past murders.
Asks whether a sin known after Yom Kippur would require no sin offering, given God's sole knowledge.
Rabbi Zeira cites the threefold term of knowing for individual, Nasi and community offerings; each is needed, so the derivation fails.
Suggests the term of knowing might be written only for a Nasi and derived for the others.
Refutes each such derivation by a distinct feature: lenient hearing-a-voice exemption, female offerings, or unwitting communal ruling.
Suggests deriving one term of knowing from the other two, by writing it only for an individual.
Refutes this: the Nasi and community offerings are exempt from hearing-a-voice liability, unlike the individual's.
Suggests the community's term of knowing be derived from the individual and Nasi offerings.
Refutes this too: individual and Nasi offerings have female cases, which the community offering lacks.
Suggests the Nasi's term of knowing be derived from the other two, and tests the refutation factors against that case.
The examples show the term of knowing is needed for the Nasi itself, so it applies to a sin found after Yom Kippur.
Abaye argues the Nasi needs a written term of knowing, since individual and community offerings are both fixed and unchanging.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the Nasi, whose offering may change if he is disqualified, should bring an individual's sin offering.
Abaye derives from the verbal analogy of mitzvot that the three sin offering cases are derived from one another.
Asks why the term of knowing is written three times if the cases are already derived, and suggests it applies after Yom Kippur.
Raises a difficulty: if a provisional offering atones for the specific sin, a later-known sin should need no sin offering.
Rava cites the verse that a known sin requires a sin offering in any case.
Asks why a provisional offering is brought at all, if a sin offering is required once the sin is known.
Rabbi Zeira says death without known iniquity; Rava says the provisional offering protects the sinner from suffering until the sin offering.
Mishna on a bird sin offering brought in doubt about a birth, which is buried if found unneeded; Rav says it atones after sprinkling.
Asks that if the bird atones, why the mishna says it must be buried rather than eaten.
Buried by rabbinic decree to prevent the bird being eaten; the mishna refers to cases of later knowledge, and Rav's statement relates to the earlier ruling.
Rav says the bird is permitted after sprinkling, while Rabbi Yohanan says it stays forbidden by rabbinic decree.
Levi's baraita supports Rav: after sprinkling the bird atones and is permitted.
Baraita supporting Rabbi Yohanan: if the offering is known not to be needed it is released or sold; otherwise it is prohibited.
Mishna on a guilt offering: two sela buy two rams, one sacrificed as guilt offering and the other sold, or misuse with a fifth added.
Asks what the term his misuse refers to in the first clause of the mishna.
Objects that the fifth must be brought with the guilt ram, but the verse says it is added to the restitution, so the reading fails.
His misuse refers to the restitution for benefit derived from consecrated property, not to the guilt ram.
Asks why the same term in the latter clause would then refer to the guilt ram, given the first-clause reading.
Notes that the mishna's repayment of one sela and a fifth shows the term refers to the guilt ram, which conflicts with the first clause.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States the contrast: the first clause uses his misuse for the restitution, the latter for the guilt ram.
Explains the contrast: a bigger ram worth principal plus a fifth matches the restitution, while a smaller ram does not.
Rav Menashya bar Gadda asks whether one who accumulated fifths totaling two sela may atone with that money.
Lays out both sides of the dilemma: whether enhancement of consecrated property can atone, depending on whether the owner exerted himself.
Suggests a proof from the mishna: a ram worth two sela after purchase is valid, implying enhancement atones.
Rejects the proof: the mishna concerns a ram bought at a discount, not one that appreciated on its own.
Suggests a proof from the baraita on fattening a ram bought for one sela, which becomes valid at two sela.
Rejects it: the fattening case differs, since expenses of eight dinars were lost, unlike an animal appreciating on its own.
Suggests a further baraita proof about a ram bought for one sela that then appreciated to two sela.
Objects that this would duplicate the first clause of that baraita.
Explains the two clauses: in the first the owner spent money to fatten, in the latter the ram gained one dinar on its own.
Objects that the latter clause should not require paying one sela, and the Gemara answers that the payment must be completed.
Asks what the one dinar matters if enhancement does not atone, since no two-sela ram exists here.
Concludes the Tosefta tanna holds that enhancement of consecrated property does atone.
Objects that if the ram is now worth two sela, he should not need to pay the one dinar.
The payment is a rabbinic decree, lest people think a ram worth less than two sela atones.
Asks what halakhic conclusion was reached on whether enhancement atones.
Baraita: a ram worth one sela at designation but two at atonement does not fulfill the obligation, so enhancement does not atone.
Rabbi Elazar raises the same dilemma, and Rabbi Yohanan rebukes him for not having heard the ruling from him.
Asks whether one may conclude from this that Rabbi Yohanan did state the halakha on this point.
Yes; a mishna on the offspring of a thanks offering supports Rabbi Yohanan's ruling.
Rabbi Hanina's letter in Rabbi Yohanan's name: the offspring needs no loaves only if sacrificed after the mother's atonement.
Thus Rabbi Yohanan holds that enhancement of consecrated property atones, since the offspring counts as enhancement.
Rabbi Elazar asks whether disqualified consecrated living animals are permanently disqualified, and Rabbi Yohanan again rebukes him.
Asks whether one may conclude by inference that Rabbi Yohanan stated the halakha on this matter.
Yes: Rabbi Yohanan rules that a half-consecrated animal bought and consecrated by one partner is consecrated but not fit to sacrifice.
Three halakhot follow: living consecrated animals can be permanently disqualified, value sanctity disqualifies a substitute, and monetary consecration disqualifies.
Rabbi Elazar asks what to do if lambs depreciate so that no two-sela ram is available, and Rabbi Yohanan says he never heard this.
Objects with Rabbi Yohanan's citation of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, that the Torah fixed the value of offerings for those lacking atonement.
Replies that Rabbi Yohanan may have said he had not taught this halakha in the study hall.
Objects that Rabbi Zeira reviewed his studies before Rabbi Yohanan every thirty days, so the halakha would have been heard.
Replies that the halakha was never asked of Rabbi Yohanan in the study hall.
Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai: the Torah set no fixed value because lamb prices could fall below it.
Abaye and Rava object by analogy with the sin offering for fat and the nazirite guilt offering, and the Gemara calls the matter difficult.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a son may not bring his father's designated sin offering, and an offering designated for one sin may not be used for another.
Asks from where the rule that a son cannot bring his father's sin offering is derived.
Baraita: the verse says bring his own offering, so one fulfills the obligation only with his own offering.
Baraita continues: the repeated wording excludes a son's use of his father's animal even for similar sins, including nazirite offerings.
Baraita: money designated by a father cannot be used by the son for a similar sin, though his own designated money works.
Baraita: the verse requires the offering to be designated for the specific sin, so swapping between lenient and severe sins fails.
Baraita: money designated for oneself also must be used for the specific sin, since misuse of Temple property would otherwise atone.
The verse again requires the offering to be for the sake of the specific sin, applying to designated money as well.
Asks what is meant by the baraita's phrase that one has not misused consecrated property and does not atone.
Rav Shmuel bar Shimi explains: an animal consecrated for the altar cannot be desacralized, so it cannot atone for another sin, while money can be misused and so is restricted from the outset.
Mishna on sliding-scale offerings: a goat may be bought with lamb money, a lamb with goat money, and birds or fine flour as one's means change.
Asks from where the mishna's rules on sliding-scale offerings are derived.
Baraita derives the sliding-scale substitutions from the verses about the sin offering, showing the rule applies to money designated for each offering.
Baraita gives examples: one who becomes poorer or wealthier with designated money brings a bird, fine flour, a lamb or a goat.
Since birds cannot be redeemed, the verse writes from his sin and over his sin to fix the rules for each case.
The verse repeats the phrase for birds because otherwise one might think money designated for a lamb could be used for a bird.
Without the repeated phrase for birds, one might think money designated for a bird pair cannot be used for fine flour, which is not a blood offering.
The repeated phrase for birds shows that money designated for birds may also be used for fine flour.
The phrase over his sin for fine flour shows that a rich person adds to his designated money to bring a bird or a lamb or goat.
The verses on rich and poor cases are read together, so the designated money is used toward the more expensive offering.
Rabbi Elazar, in the name of Rabbi Oshaya, says a wealthy person who defiles the Temple brings a lamb or goat according to his means.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the ruling that a sacrifice disqualified at the outset because of a lamb obligation is permanently disqualified.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua derives three halakhot from that ruling, including permanent disqualification of living consecrated animals.
Rav Ukva bar Hama objects from a baraita on a female Paschal animal and its male offspring, which must be sold.
Rabbi Shimon says the offspring itself is sacrificed, so consecrated living animals are not permanently disqualified.
Rabbi Oshaya's school says permanent disqualification applies only in the view of the Rabbis, who do not sacrifice the offspring, while Rabbi Shimon holds otherwise.
Rabbi Shimon holds the lottery for the two Yom Kippur goats is not indispensable, which implies living animals are not permanently disqualified.
Rav Hisda says nests of birds are designated as burnt or sin offerings either by the owner at purchase or by the priest at sacrifice.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi grounds Rav Hisda's rule in verses on the childbirth and leper offerings, which name the two birds in sequence.
Objects with a Sifra baraita: drawing lots makes the Yom Kippur goat a sin offering, while verbal designation does not.
Derives the halakha as a fortiori: if verbal designation sanctifies a birds case, it should sanctify the goats, but the verse excludes it.
The baraita concludes that the verse excludes verbal designation for the goats, so the lot alone makes the sin offering.
Explains the objection: verbal designation is like the lot, which takes no effect at purchase or sacrifice, contrary to Rav Hisda, and Rav reads the baraita to fit.
The verse on the lot and the verbal designation shows that the lot alone sanctifies, supporting Rav's reading.
Objects with a baraita on a poor man who defiled the Temple and designated money for birds, who must now bring a lamb or goat.
Baraita: if he designated money for a sin offering and a burnt offering, he adds to the sin offering money but not from the burnt offering money.
Explains that the baraita refers to a designation made outside purchase or sacrifice, which still establishes the money's status.
Rav Sheshet objects: a wealthy man who brings a poor person's offering does not fulfill his obligation, so his designation cannot fix the money.
The baraita refers to a designation made while he was still poor, so there is no difficulty for Rav Hisda.
Asks how the baraita is read if Rabbi Hagga holds a wealthy person who brings a poor offering has fulfilled his obligation.
The baraita should be taught as: after becoming wealthier he bought animals and designated them at purchase.
Objects with a baraita on lepers: a poor leper's offering for a wealthy person suffices, but a wealthy leper's for a poor person does not, refuting Rabbi Hagga.
Rabbi Hagga can reply the leper's case differs, since the verse this is the law of the leper limits him to the appropriate offering.
Objects that the verse would then limit even poor lepers, and cites the baraita that the law of the leper includes a poor leper who brought a rich offering.
Asks why a general principle is not derived from that verse for all sliding-scale offerings.
The verse and his in the leper law limit the rule to lepers, while one who defiles the Temple fulfills his obligation with the rich-for-poor offering.
Mishna: Rabbi Shimon says lambs precede goats in the Torah, but the verses show both are equal.
Mishna: doves precede pigeons in most places, but the reversed verse shows they are equal.
Mishna: the father precedes the mother in honor, but the verse reverses the order to show equal honor; the Sages hold the father takes precedence.
Mishna continues: the teacher takes precedence over the father in honor, since the son and father are both obligated to honor the teacher.
Baraita: the Temple courtyard cried four cries, the first demanding removal of the sons of Eli who defiled the Sanctuary.
Second cry: the gates should open for Yohanan ben Nedavai, who ate four se'a of doves, the cry being that he ate meat of consecrated offerings.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Says that in all the days of Yohanan ben Nedavai no sacrificial meat was ever left over in the courtyard.
Third cry: the gates open for Elishama ben Pikai, a student of Pinehas, who is worthy of the High Priesthood.
Fourth cry: Yissakhar of Barkai is expelled for honoring himself and dishonoring sacred items by wrapping his hands in silk.
Asks what ultimately happened to Yissakhar of Barkai.
Narrates that King Yannai and the queen asked Yissakhar, the High Priest, whether goat or lamb meat is better.
Yissakhar answers with a gesture that displeases the king, who orders his hands cut off; Rav Yosef sees the punishment as fitting.
Rav Ashi says Yissakhar did not learn the mishna on lambs preceding goats, which the verses show are equal.
Ravina says Yissakhar did not even read the Torah, since both lamb and goat peace offerings are permitted.
Rabbi Elazar, in Rabbi Hanina's name, says scholars increase peace in the world, reading banayikh as builders.
Closes the chapter and the tractate Keritot.
